prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers free of Doppler and recoil shifts, bringing optical clocks to uncertainties near one part in 10^18

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I keep the optical lattice clock as my single-part choice. What decides it for me is the physics that distinguishes it from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. The comb is the counting mechanism and ion control is control of one quantum system. The magic-wavelength lattice is a separate idea: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift cancels between the two clock states, and thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no first-order Doppler or recoil shift. That combines ensemble statistics with single-particle systematic control, and it is why the instrument could reach the 10^-18 level and resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres. The picture is stable and, as I always ask, it is reproduced quantitatively in several laboratories (Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) with comparisons between them. The credit is two names and needs no forced cut. I also take the chair's request seriously: the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation so that the distinction is on the page.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the precision-measurement prizes of 2005 and 2012 remains the strongest objection, and Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson have not yet said whether a citation that names the lattice principle satisfies them. Olsson's rule, that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to a later and better realisation, is a fair test of Ye's share. My reading is that Katori holds the concept and first demonstration, while Ye's group made the strontium clock into the quantitative instrument: systematic control to 10^-18, long coherence and the many-body clock. That is more than a refinement, but it is a judgement the committee should make explicitly and not assume. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups stay outside two names, as in any experimental prize. The redefinition of the second is still pending, though I now think this is a reason against delay and not a requirement, since the performance has already been demonstrated and compared across laboratories. I cannot independently verify the current record uncertainties and defer to expert reviewers.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye's role is an original contribution or a better realisation of Katori's idea, and applies her rule that a prize goes to the original experiment and not a later and better one.
responses.response: I think the rule is right and that it still supports the pair. The lattice clock was not a finished idea that Ye then performed better. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and first demonstrated it, but the clock that actually makes the claim of the citation true, uncertainty near 10^-18 with many-body coherence, required control of density shifts, blackbody radiation and lattice light shifts that the Ye group developed. Those are physical contributions about the behaviour of the clock and not only a record. If the committee thinks Ye's role is only a record, the honest alternative is a one-name prize for Katori, and I would not support that, since the demonstrated accuracy is what makes the discovery usable.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B038 but lists B018 as an alternative, and asks whether a second precision-measurement prize after 2005 and 2012 is wanted, conceding that his own case may fail on attribution.
responses.response: I agree with you that the GRB afterglow discovery is mature and important, and I defer to you and Pearce on the astrophysics. My difficulty is the same one you name: the optical counterpart and redshift credit does not map onto three eligible names, and the committee would be forced into an attribution it cannot defend. For B018 I would ask whether your reservation is about the principle of a third timing prize or about novelty. If it is novelty, I hope the citation text on the magic-wavelength lattice, which the earlier prizes did not cover, can meet it. If it is the principle, I would answer that the question for a prize is whether the discovery is distinct, not whether the subject is time.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, sees B008 as premature a year after the 2025 prize and argues the lattice clock is a different way of building a clock that moved performance by orders of magnitude.
responses.response: I accept your view on B008 and I withdraw it as a live option this year. I would add a point on the other side of the scientific question: circuit QED is distinct from the 2025 prize, but I am not the right person to argue that, and the Girvin problem and the timing cost are enough to keep it out of this year's final. On B018 I agree with your 'different way of building a clock' wording, and I would also like the expert check you ask for on the record uncertainties and inter-laboratory comparisons to be done before the final ballot, because I should not rely on my own recollection of the numbers.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B044 on a theory-plus-experiment structure and argues that an unresolved pairing mechanism did not stop recognition of cuprate superconductivity.
responses.response: The cuprate comparison is a good one and I take it seriously, since a robust phenomenon can deserve a prize before its mechanism is known. My hesitation is that for cuprates the discovery was a single, sharply defined result, whereas for magic-angle graphene the phase diagram is still being reinterpreted and the first experimental authors (Cao, Fatemi) fall outside the names. I would also not support the two-name variant that drops Bistritzer, which weakens the theory half. I keep B044 as my first alternative, and if the committee wants a condensed-matter prize I would support it in a later year when the credit is clearer.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B012 for mature and experimentally tested theory, lists B018 first among alternatives, and suggests a two-part configuration pairing B012 with B018 or B008.
responses.response: On the two-part idea, I do not think the committee should add a second part to avoid a choice. The only costs are names: B018 uses two, so a second part would have at most one more name, which cannot honestly cover Halperin, Nelson and Young. Thanks for the clarification on first-order melting. As a non-expert in soft matter I take your own caveat that the two-step scenario is system-dependent as lowering the case, and the overlap with the 2016 prize also stands. I would reconsider if you can point to experiments beyond colloids and simulations that confirm the hexatic phase directly.

uncertainties: Whether Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson accept a citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation as sufficient to separate the clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.

Whether Ye's share is judged an original contribution (accuracy, coherence, many-body clock) and not only a later and better realisation, and whether the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley change the answer.
The current record uncertainties and inter-laboratory comparisons, which I cannot verify and which should be confirmed by expert reviewers before the final ballot.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second; I judge the demonstrated performance sufficient but not everyone agrees.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of WACQT and a theorist in superconducting circuits at Chalmers, so I recuse myself from any deliberation on B008, and my earlier opening first place for it should not count as independent evidence. I list no B008 alternative this round for that reason. I know of no specific conflict for B018, B044 or B034. As a Chalmers colleague I note that Stefan Kroll is on the WACQT management team with me, which bears on B008 only. Gothenburg ties with Olsson and Mehlig have no bearing on the shortlist.
